title: Professional Ethics for Aerospace Engineers
subtitle: A discussion course for third-year B.Tech students on how engineering catastrophes are produced by ordinary people following ordinary incentives, and on keeping the path from evidence to decision open while it is still cheap to do so.
startNote: This course ran from 29 August to 31 October 2026. Sessions run on discussion, not lecture: each is built around a brief of a real situation that stops at the point where somebody had to decide.
modulesLead: Six sessions. Students read a brief and commit to a written position before each session; what actually happened is disclosed only after the room has argued it.

modules.title: I. “Safety is pure waste” — 29 Aug
items: What happens when the institutions that check engineers are removed

modules.title: II. Evidence and the path to decision — 5 Sep
items: The evidence almost always exists beforehand; what fails is the path from it to the decision

modules.title: III. Certification, delegated authority and many hands — 19 Sep
items: Responsibility when no single person decided the thing that went wrong

modules.title: IV. Speaking up — 10 Oct
items: Raising a concern early, in writing, while it is cheap

modules.title: V. Integrity in analysis and simulation — 24 Oct
items: What gets left out of a report, and who signs it

modules.title: VI. What a profession is — 31 Oct
items: Codes read last, as an audit of the cases studied

assessmentLead: Sixty per cent of the marks are for spoken, group or presented work, and there is no examination.

assessment.d: One handwritten paragraph before each session; marked on submission, not content
One after each session, 300 words; best five of six count
Twelve minutes, once in the semester
Across all six sessions; written contributions count
Framing memo (5%), group presentation (15%) and report (15%) on a case not taught in the course

rules: Grades are absolute; passing requires 40% overall and attendance at four of the six sessions.
Pre-session positions are handwritten in the room and cannot be submitted late.
AI tools are permitted for assignments as a supplement, with the prompt and changes declared.
Groups are assigned, not chosen; two groups open every session.
